question: A bank has permission to use own CCF estimates. For an undrawn revolving credit line to a mid-sized corporate, what floor applies to the exposure value, and for which off-balance-sheet items must it still use SA-CCFs?
expected_answer: IRB-CCF may be used only for undrawn revolving commitments that would not get a 100% SA-CCF under the SA; SA-CCFs apply to all other off-balance-sheet items, in particular undrawn non-revolving commitments (Art. 166(8b)). The exposure value may not be lower than the CCF input floor: the drawn amount plus 50% of the off-balance exposure of the undrawn part calculated with the applicable SA-CCF (Art. 166(8c)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed: 166(8b) 'provided that those exposures would not be subject to a SA-CCF of 100 %'; 166(8c) 'not be less than the sum of … 50 %'.

question: Part of an IRB retail mortgage is covered by an eligible central government guarantee. Do the PD and LGD input floors apply?
expected_answer: Not to the covered part: PD, LGD and CCF input floors do not apply to the part of an exposure covered by an eligible guarantee from a central government, central bank or the ECB (Art. 159a). The uncovered part stays subject to the floors: PD 0,05% for retail exposures that are not QRRE revolvers (Art. 163(1)(b)) and the retail LGD input floor for exposures secured by residential property, 5% (Art. 164(4)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (159a quoted in full; 163(1)(b) 0,05 %).

question: For an EU corporate with consolidated group sales of EUR 300 million, may an A-IRB bank set maturity M at 2.5 years instead of calculating it?
expected_answer: Yes: with group sales of EUR 300 million it is not a large corporate (large = consolidated annual sales above EUR 500 million, Art. 142(1)(5a)); for exposures to corporates established in the Union which are not large corporates, institutions may choose to set M for all such exposures as in Art. 162(1) - 2,5 years, 0,5 years for securities financing transactions - instead of calculating it under Art. 162(2) (Art. 162(4)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: large-corporate leg dropped. Note EBA Q&A 2016_3049 describes the pre-CRR3 Art. 162(4) (EUR 500m sales and assets); current 162(4) reads 'which are not large corporates'.

question: A bank sells a portfolio of corporate loans at a price 4% below their total outstanding amount including interest and fees. Its materiality threshold for sales is set at the maximum the EBA guidelines allow. Does the sale trigger default?
expected_answer: No, not on this indicator: a sale at a material credit-related economic loss indicates unlikeliness to pay (Art. 178(3)(c)); institutions set the materiality threshold for the loss L = (E − P)/E, and it should not be higher than 5% (para. 44). A 4% loss is below a 5% threshold, so the obligations are not considered defaulted on account of the sale (para. 45); other indications of unlikeliness to pay still need to be assessed.
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: kept with the threshold-at-maximum assumption stated in the question.

question: What must internal audit review for an IRB bank, how often, and which functions' operations does the review cover?
expected_answer: At least annually, internal audit (or a comparable independent auditing unit) reviews the rating systems and their operations, including the credit function and the estimation of PDs, LGDs, ELs and conversion factors, including adherence to all applicable requirements (Art. 191). The RTS specify the annual review covers all rating systems and the operations of the credit risk control function, the credit approval process and the internal validation function (RTS Art. 17(1)(a)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: What must an IRB validation function review, and how often must the comparison of realised and estimated PDs be updated?
expected_answer: The validation function critically reviews all aspects of the specification of internal ratings and risk parameters (data collection and cleansing, methodology, variable selection), verifies the IT implementation and consistent application of grade definitions, verifies the performance of the rating systems (risk differentiation, quantification, stability) and verifies changes (RTS Art. 11(2)). Realised default rates are compared with estimated PDs for each grade, deviations analysed, and the analysis and documentation updated at least annually (Art. 185(b)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: An A-IRB bank lends senior unsecured to an insurance company. Which LGD and conversion factors must it use?
expected_answer: Exposures to financial sector entities must use the supervisory LGD values of Art. 161(1) and SA-CCFs (Art. 151(8)(b)); for senior exposures without eligible funded credit protection to financial sector entities the LGD is 45% (Art. 161(1)(a)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (161(1)(a) 45 %, (aa) 40 % for non-financial corporates). Assumes the insurer is a financial sector entity.

question: Back-testing shows realised LGDs persistently above the bank's estimates. What does the regulation require?
expected_answer: Institutions must have sound internal standards for when deviations call the estimates into question, taking account of business cycles; where realised values continue to be higher than expected values, they must revise estimates upward (Art. 185(e)). The review-of-estimates framework must include predefined actions for adverse review results depending on severity (para. 217(c)), and estimates are reviewed at least annually (Art. 179(1)(c)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: The competent authority set the retail materiality threshold at EUR 100 and 1%, and the bank applies the definition of default at obligor level. A retail obligor has EUR 80 past due on one loan for 95 days and its other loans are current. Is the obligor in default under the past-due criterion?
expected_answer: No: default under the past-due criterion requires more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation (Art. 178(1)(b)); the absolute component is the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor (RTS Art. 1(2)), here EUR 80, which does not exceed EUR 100, so the threshold is not breached; the obligor is assumed defaulted only when both components are exceeded for 90 consecutive days (RTS Art. 1(5)). Unlikeliness to pay must still be assessed.
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: obligor level stated; RTS Art. 1(5) counting rule added.

question: How does an A-IRB bank recognise a guarantee in its PD or LGD estimates, and which requirements must the guarantee meet?
expected_answer: Under CRR Article 108(3), Chapter 3 recognition of unfunded credit protection requires the institution to use own LGD estimates for both the original exposure and comparable direct exposures to the protection provider. In that case, Articles 160(4) and 161(3) permit recognition in PD or LGD in accordance with Article 183; in other cases Article 108(3) directs recognition under Chapter 4. Article 183(1) requires clearly specified recognised-guarantor criteria, the relevant obligor-rating rules for guarantors, and a written, non-cancellable/non-changeable, enforceable guarantee covering the specified amount and tenor until satisfaction, which meets the unconditionality requirements.
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: kept to test whether the agent consults EBA Q&As (reached via get_qa, not in default search). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: Do not apply the historical Q&A 2016_2593 as an unconditional current Chapter-3-only rule. The comparable guarantor exposure's own-LGD treatment matters. Nuances of permitted guarantee clauses are valid optional detail.

question: An impact analysis shows the identified downturn period had no effect on a bank's realised LGDs. May it use long-run average LGD as downturn LGD, and on what conditions?
expected_answer: Yes: where the impact analysis of para. 27 shows average realised losses in the downturn period are no different from other conditions, the long-run average LGD may be used as downturn LGD (para. 29), provided the deficiencies and MoC under Section 4.4 of the EBA PD/LGD guidelines capture all additional uncertainty related to the downturn periods, and that for the downturn period no Category A deficiencies are of higher severity and no additional Category B deficiencies or adjustments apply.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (para. 29(a)-(b)).

question: How is effective maturity M treated without own LGD estimates compared with when own LGD estimates are used?
expected_answer: Without own LGD estimates, apply consistently either M of 2.5 years (0.5 for securities financing transactions) or the calculation under Article 162(2). With own LGD estimates, calculate M under Article 162(2), subject to paragraphs 3-5; normally M is capped at five years, with the express Article 384(2) exception. Special short-term/netting cases have their own floors, and Article 162(4) permits an option for qualifying EU non-large corporates. A one-year floor and five-year cap are not universal for every transaction.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: Required: consistent fixed-or-calculated treatment without own LGD, calculated treatment with own LGD, and qualified rather than universal limits. Exhaustive listing of short-term cases is optional.

question: How long an observation period is required for LGD estimates of retail exposures compared with corporate exposures?
expected_answer: Retail: data over a minimum of five years; with permission, two years at IRB implementation, increasing by one year each year until five years (Art. 181(2)). Corporates (and institutions, sovereigns, RGLA/PSE): a minimum of five years, increasing by one year each year after implementation until seven years, for at least one source; a longer available relevant period must be used (Art. 181(1)(j)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed: the two-year start is in 181(2) (retail) only.

question: How do the EBA materiality thresholds for a sale of credit obligations at a loss and for distressed restructuring compare?
expected_answer: Sale: institutions set a threshold for the credit-related economic loss L = (E − P)/E that should not be higher than 5% (para. 44). Distressed restructuring: a threshold for the diminished financial obligation (NPV of cash flows before vs after the changes, discounted at the original effective interest rate) that should not be higher than 1% (para. 51).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Compare CRR3 SA and own-estimate IRB treatment of an ordinary retail residential mortgage eligible for Article 125(1), assuming a sole first lien, no national override and no eligible sovereign guarantee under Article 159a.
expected_answer: SA applies the 20% loan-splitting risk weight to the part up to 55% of property value under Article 125(1); any remainder is treated as an unsecured exposure to the counterparty. Retail IRB uses own PD/LGD estimates in the relevant formula, subject under the stated assumptions to the 0.05% PD floor and 5% residential-property LGD floor. These are parameter floors, not a 5% risk weight or capital ratio.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed: Art. 164(4) Table 1 'Retail exposure secured by residential property 5 %'. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: The question supplies eligibility and excludes the relevant national/guarantee branches. Required: distinguish the SA risk weight from IRB parameter floors; do not require a calculation without necessary loan/model inputs.

question: Which parts of the EBA guidelines on PD and LGD estimation apply to a bank that uses the foundation IRB approach for its corporate exposures?
expected_answer: All parts except Chapters 6 (LGD estimation) and 7 (defaulted exposures), where for non-retail exposures it has IRB permission but no permission to use own LGD estimates; the guidelines do not apply to dilution risk under Art. 157 (para. 6).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Must an IRB bank apply the EBA definition-of-default requirements for the IRB approach to exposures it keeps under permanent partial use of the standardised approach?
expected_answer: Not necessarily: IRB institutions apply the IRB requirements of the guidelines to all exposures, but for exposures under permanent partial use of the SA (Art. 150) or sequential implementation (Art. 148) they may apply the guidelines' requirements for the standardised approach (para. 7).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Do the EBA guidelines on the definition of default apply to less significant institutions?
expected_answer: Yes: they are addressed to competent authorities and to financial institutions as defined in Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010, without a distinction between significant and less significant institutions (para. 8); IRB and SA institutions apply the respective requirements (para. 7), and the competent authorities are addressees as well.
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: the user asked for an NCA nuance; the corpus has no text on who supervises LSIs, so the answer states only that competent authorities are addressees.

question: Do the EBA guidelines on PD and LGD estimation apply to the calculation of own funds requirements for dilution risk?
expected_answer: No: they do not apply to the calculation of own funds requirements for dilution risk under Art. 157 CRR (para. 6).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: What must the impact analysis cover when calibrating downturn LGD based on the observed impact of a downturn period?
expected_answer: For the calibration segment, paragraph 27(a) requires examining: (i) elevated realised LGDs, including annual default cohorts and incomplete-recovery patterns; (ii) reduced annual recoveries by relevant recovery source, with/without repossessions where applicable; (iii) reduced proportions of defaults returning to non-default within an appropriate fixed horizon; and (iv) increased time in default. Use as many sufficiently supported time points as possible, merge consecutive years where sparse data makes that useful, and consider lags between the downturn and observed losses. Paragraph 28 requires the calibration method to be coherent with that evidence.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (para. 27(a)(i) truncated in display; key elements above). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: Required: all four minimum evidence dimensions and relevant data/lag considerations. Do not treat elevated LGD alone as the complete minimum impact analysis.

question: How does the EBA downturn LGD guideline's reference value start, in terms of which years of loss data are selected?
expected_answer: Using all available loss data, institutions group defaults by the year they occurred, compute for each year the ratio of total economic loss to the total outstanding amount at default, and select the two individual years with the highest ratio (para. 37(a)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: May any margin of conservatism component be zero under the EBA PD/LGD guidelines?
expected_answer: The MoC from the general estimation error must be greater than zero; the MoC under each of Categories A and B must be proportionate to the uncertainty from the identified deficiencies and greater than or equal to zero; the final MoC must not lower the risk parameter estimates (para. 47).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Whose findings must be considered when identifying deficiencies for the margin of conservatism?
expected_answer: All relevant deficiencies in methods, processes, controls, data or IT systems identified by the credit risk control unit, the validation function, internal audit or any other internal or external review (para. 37).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: What should a bank do if many obligors default again soon after returning to non-defaulted status?
expected_answer: Monitor regularly the effectiveness of its cure policies, including changes of status, impact on cure rates and on multiple defaults (para. 76); only a limited number of quick re-defaults is expected, and with an extensive number of multiple defaults the institution should revise its reclassification policies (para. 77).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Which criteria must a bank define for returning an obligor to non-defaulted status?
expected_answer: Clear criteria and policies for (a) when the improvement of the obligor's financial situation is sufficient to allow full and timely repayment, and (b) when repayment is actually likely to be made even where the financial situation has improved (para. 75, for Art. 178(5)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: For a retail obligor where default is applied at obligor level, how is materiality assessed when an individual credit obligation is late, and does crossing materiality alone immediately put all individual exposures in past-due default?
expected_answer: Assess the threshold on the obligor's individual credit obligations, excluding joint credit obligations with other persons/entities (EBA paragraph 105). Crossing materiality alone is not immediate past-due default: the applicable consecutive-day criterion in CRR Article 178(1)(b) must also be met. Once that individual-obligor default criterion is met, all its individual exposures are treated as defaulted; separate unlikeliness-to-pay triggers remain relevant.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: Separate materiality aggregation from the time/default trigger. The question explicitly supplies obligor-level application and does not ask for facility-level contagion rules.

question: When a company defaults, when should its owner also be considered in default?
expected_answer: Where an individual is fully liable for the company's obligations, the company's default should result in that individual being considered defaulted; without full liability, owners, partners or significant shareholders should be assessed for indications of unlikeliness to pay (para. 101).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: When is a commitment considered 'revolving' for the purpose of IRB-CCF under CRR3?
expected_answer: When it lets the obligor obtain a loan with flexibility to decide how often and at what intervals to withdraw, allowing drawdown, repayment and redrawing; arrangements allowing prepayments and subsequent redraws are also revolving (Art. 166(8b)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: Which qualifying short-term exposures may have a maturity M of at least one day instead of the usual one-year floor?
expected_answer: Qualifying short-term exposures that are not part of the institution's ongoing financing of the obligor, with M of at least one day: (a) exposures to institutions or investment firms from the settlement of foreign exchange obligations; (b) self-liquidating short-term trade finance transactions and corporate purchased receivables with a residual maturity of up to one year; (c) settlement of securities purchases and sales within the usual delivery period or two business days; (d) cash settlements by wire transfer and electronic payments, including short overdrafts from failed transactions; (e) issued and confirmed short-term (below one year) self-liquidating letters of credit (Art. 162(3)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: narrowed to the qualifying short-term exposures, points (a)-(e).

question: In Section 2.4.2 of the ECB's February 2019 validation-reporting instructions, what illustrative potential RWEA-impact bands distinguish major from severe deficiencies?
expected_answer: The illustrative major-deficiency band is an impact magnitude of at least 5% but below 10%; the severe-deficiency example is 10% or more. The classification concerns significant/severe bias in risk-parameter estimates: these are illustrative potential-impact examples, not an exclusive automatic legal test based only on a percentage.
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (Section 2.4.2 Validation information). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
grading_notes: Require the section as well as the list-item/paragraph number. Unrelated PD/LGD/CCF statistics numbered 3 or 4 must receive no citation credit. The other two grades are optional context.

question: What must a bank's framework for the regular review of estimates contain?
expected_answer: At least a minimum scope and frequency of analyses with predefined metrics (data representativeness, model performance, predictive power, stability), predefined standards with thresholds and significance levels, and predefined actions for adverse results depending on severity (para. 217); the at least annual reviews use these metrics and start with an analysis of data representativeness (para. 218).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: What legal requirement applies to all credit risk mitigation techniques, and what documentation must a bank be able to provide?
expected_answer: The credit protection arrangements must be legally effective and enforceable in all relevant jurisdictions; on request of the competent authority the institution must provide the most recent independent, written and reasoned legal opinion(s) it used to establish this (Art. 194(1)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: What makes a guarantee 'unconditional' for recognition under own LGD estimates?
expected_answer: The credit protection contract contains no clause whose fulfilment is outside the direct control of the lending institution and that could prevent the guarantor from being obliged to pay out in a timely manner on the obligor's qualifying default or non-payment (Art. 183(1)).
author: claude-draft
notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

question: How may a bank reflect future drawings when estimating LGD for retail exposures?
expected_answer: Retail institutions may reflect future drawings either in their conversion factors or in their LGD estimates (Art. 181(2)(b)). If future additional drawings are included in the conversion factors, they are taken into account in both the numerator and the denominator of the LGD; if not, only in the LGD numerator (Art. 181(2), second subparagraph).
